verses.translation_literal: Praise [obj] YHWH, all [you] nations; extol him, all [you] peoples.
verses.translation_dramatic: Praise the LORD — all you nations, praise him! Lift his name high, all you peoples, every one of you, from every side of the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
Stand the actors well apart. This is the shortest psalm in the book, two verses, and it compresses into that space a summons the Psalter has made before: to the nations in Psalm 47:2 ("clap your hands, all you peoples"), 66:1, 96:7 and 100:1 ("all you lands"). Here the summons is the whole psalm, with nothing else around it. The voice turns outward to the goyim, the foreign nations, who elsewhere in the Psalter often appear as enemies, as a threat, or as the stage on which Israel's God shows his power. The actor must speak to a crowd that is not in the room.

The verse is built as a pair. Hebrew poetry says a thing and then says it again with a different word: הַלְלוּ and שַׁבְּחוּ (praise / extol), גּוֹיִם and אֻמִּים (nations / peoples). The KJV flattens this to "praise ... praise" and "nations ... people", and its singular "people" blurs the plural אֻמִּים, a rare word, so the sense of 'all the peoples of the earth, tribe by tribe' is lost. Notice also that the KJV writes "the Lord" where the Hebrew has the four letters of the divine name, YHWH, the personal name of Israel's God. The nations are being asked to name Israel's God, not a generic deity. In a world where every nation had its own gods, and honoured them with temples and kings, that is a startling demand. Radak (on Psalm 117:1) reads it as a future hope, when every nation will join Israel; Malbim reads it as a call to the captives of Sennacherib. The psalm itself does not say.

philological_notes.note: Plural imperative of הלל, 'to praise, boast about', the root that gives 'Hallelujah' (הַלְלוּ־יָהּ). Here it is addressed to foreigners, which gives the familiar word a sharper edge.

Plural imperative of שבח (Piel), 'to commend, to laud', with the object 'him' attached. The Targum uses שבח for both verbs (שַׁבְּחוּ ... שַׁבַּחוּ ליה), so, like the KJV, it does not keep the two Hebrew verbs distinct. Radak notes that the verse doubles the idea in different words.
A rare plural of אֻמָּה, 'people, clan'. It occurs seldom, so the pairing with גּוֹיִם works as an intensifier: not a different group, but the same crowd counted another way.

verses.translation_literal: For his steadfast love has prevailed over us, and the faithfulness of YHWH is for ever. Praise Yah!
verses.translation_dramatic: For his steadfast love has risen over us and held, and the LORD's faithfulness does not end. It stands for ever. Praise the LORD!
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the reason clause, and the whole psalm turns on it. The word כִּי, 'for', explains why the nations should praise: not because of what God did to them, but because of what he did for "us". The speaker is Israel, and they are overheard making their case to the world. Play it with quiet astonishment rather than pride.

Two words carry the weight. חֶסֶד is the KJV's "merciful kindness", a two-word compound because English has no single word for it. It is closer to covenant loyalty, the steady love that holds a promise to someone who has no claim on it. אֱמֶת, the KJV's "truth", is not the opposite of falsehood but reliability: what you can lean your weight on. KJV's "great toward us" also softens the verb. גָּבַר is 'to be strong, to win out', as in a battle, so his love has literally got the upper hand over Israel's failings and enemies. Rashi (on Psalm 117:2) reads "faithfulness" as God keeping the promise he made to the fathers, and Radak points to the covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham; the other commentators fill in the historical moment differently.

The closing הַלְלוּ־יָהּ uses the short form of the divine name, Yah. KJV has "Praise ye the Lord", which loses that the psalm begins and ends on the same two verbs, with the name set between. Radak says it is repeated for emphasis, or spoken to Israel as a counterpart to the nations of verse 1.

philological_notes.note: 'To be strong, to prevail'. With עַל it can mean 'over' or 'toward', so 'his love has prevailed over us' and 'great toward us' are both possible. It is the root of גֶּבֶר, 'a strong man'.
Covenant loyalty, steadfast love, the loyalty owed or freely given inside a bond. 'Mercy' in the KJV suggests pity for the weak; חֶסֶד is closer to faithfulness that costs the giver something.
Reliability, firmness, 'what holds up'. KJV 'truth' is true but narrow. Rashi connects it to God keeping the promise made to the patriarchs.
